title: Protect the root account
brief: 18:30. An audit finds the cloud account's root user in daily use, with an access key stored in a CI variable, and no hardware security key.
role: Platform engineer, reviewing a change on the Veltrix engineering team
insight: The root account can do everything and cannot be restricted. It should barely ever be used.
teaches: The root account is for a handful of tasks: lock it away, with a hardware key
Do daily administration through roles and single sign on
Delete root access keys: they cannot be scoped down

value.title: Account security review: root user
value.intro: Act as an attacker with a foothold in the shared mailbox, then in the CI. See how far each gets.

attempts.label: Use root for an everyday task
attempts.request: sign in as root -> restart a service
attempts.response:
HTTP 200
Done. Root did a job any admin role could have done.
attempts.fixedResponse: AccessDenied: sign in as root is blocked for this action. Use your admin role.

attempts.label: Reset the root password from the shared mailbox
attempts.response:
Reset link opened. New password set.
No hardware key was asked for: an SMS code was enough.

Whoever reads that shared mailbox now owns the account that owns everything.
attempts.fixedResponse: Reset link opened. Blocked: root sign in requires the hardware security key, which the attacker does not have.

attempts.label: Use the root access key left in CI
attempts.request: deploy job: aws --profile root s3 ls
attempts.response: Every bucket in the account listed. The CI variable is a live root key.
attempts.fixedResponse: Error: no credential named 'root'. Root has no access keys.

fix.prompt: Pick every change that gets root out of daily use and locks what is left behind hardware.

options.label: Delete the root access key entirely
code: + # no access keys on the root user, ever
options.why: Root cannot be scoped down, so it should never hold a key a script or a pipeline can use.

options.label: Require a hardware security key for root, and stop accepting an SMS code for it
options.why: An SMS code can be intercepted or socially engineered. Root, which cannot be restricted, deserves the strongest factor.

options.label: Do daily administration through named roles and single sign on, and lock root away for emergencies only
code: + root: used only to recover account access, logged and alerted
options.why: Root stops being an everyday account, so a phished password or a leaked key cannot reach it through routine work.

options.label: Move root's recovery email off the shared mailbox
options.why: A shared mailbox that many people can read is not a safe place to control the account that controls everything.

options.label: Keep SMS as the second factor, but require it every time
options.why: Still phishable and interceptable. The factor is the weak point, not how often it is asked for.

outcome.label: Read the vulnerable code first
outcome.what: Reading the code before attacking it tells you where to look, and why it fails.
outcome.ideal: reads the code under review before trying to break it.

outcome.label: Tried normal use first
outcome.what: Knowing what a good request looks like is how you spot a bad one.
outcome.ideal: establishes normal behaviour before testing the abnormal.

outcome.label: Checked normal use still works
outcome.what: A fix that breaks real users gets reverted, and the bug comes back.
outcome.ideal: tests that the fix did not break normal use.

exploit.objective: Reproduce the bug: read the Code tab, then use the Exploit tab on staging.
exploit.insight: The root account can do everything and cannot be restricted. It should barely ever be used.

label: Send this request: it breaks it
Open the Exploit tab

hint.text: Open the Workbench. Read the code, try normal use on the Exploit tab, then send the request that breaks it.

outcome.label: Reproduced the bug
outcome.what: Root was used for ordinary work, its password could be reset from a mailbox several people read, and a live root key sat in a CI variable. Any one of those routes hands over an account that cannot be restricted.
outcome.ideal: proves a bug is real before fixing it.

card.title: Every door led back to root
body: Root was used for ordinary work, its password could be reset from a mailbox several people read, and a live root key sat in a CI variable. Any one of those routes hands over an account that cannot be restricted.
Root is the one identity in the account with no ceiling.
card.ideal: reproduces a bug first, so the fix can be proved to work.

fix.objective: Fix it: pick the changes on the Fix tab that close the hole for good, then apply the patch.

label: Picked everything that fixes it? Apply the patch
Pick every change that fixes the cause
Open the Fix tab

hint.text: Pick every change that removes the cause. Avoid changes an attacker can walk around, and ones that do not touch the problem. Then Apply the patch.

outcome.label: Applied a real fix
outcome.what: With no access key, a hardware only second factor, and daily work done through roles, root stops being reachable by a phished password or a leaked pipeline variable. Moving its recovery email off a shared mailbox closes the last route.
outcome.ideal: fixes the cause, not the symptom.

card.title: Locked away, reached only by hardware
body: With no access key, a hardware only second factor, and daily work done through roles, root stops being reachable by a phished password or a leaked pipeline variable. Moving its recovery email off a shared mailbox closes the last route.
Use root as little as the design of the account lets you.
card.ideal: fixes the cause with the standard control, and adds defence in depth.

outcome.label: Applied a fix that can be bypassed
outcome.what: Asking for an SMS code every time does not change that SMS can be intercepted or talked out of someone. The account with no ceiling deserves a factor that cannot be phished.
outcome.ideal: fixes the cause instead of blocking one payload or hiding the symptom.

card.title: Same weak factor, more often
body: Asking for an SMS code every time does not change that SMS can be intercepted or talked out of someone. The account with no ceiling deserves a factor that cannot be phished.
card.ideal: fixes the cause, and knows why a blocklist or a hidden field is not a fix.

outcome.label: Applied a patch that was not enough
outcome.what: The patch missed part of the fix, or added a change that does not address the problem.

card.title: Not enough
body: The patch missed something that has to change, or included a change that does nothing for this bug. Open the Fix tab to see which options were right, missed, or wrong, and why.
A partial fix is the most dangerous kind: everyone assumes it is closed.

verify.objective: Prove it: re-run the exploit on the Exploit tab, then check normal use still works.

label: Send the exploit again: it should be blocked
Open the Exploit tab

hint.text: On the Exploit tab, send the exploit again. It should be blocked. Then send the normal request to check nothing broke.

outcome.label: Proved the exploit is blocked
outcome.what: The same request that worked before now fails, and normal use still works.
outcome.ideal: verifies a fix by re-running the exploit.

card.title: Fixed, and proved
body: You re-ran the exact request that broke it, and it is blocked. A fix you have not tested against the exploit is a hope, not a fix.
Add the exploit as an automated test so nobody can quietly bring the bug back.
card.ideal: turns the exploit into a regression test.

outcome.label: The exploit still works
outcome.what: The patch did not close the hole. The same kind of request still gets through.
outcome.ideal: never ships a fix without re-running the exploit.

card.title: Still open
body: The exploit still works after your patch. This is what happens when a fix blocks one payload, or hides a symptom, instead of removing the cause.
Go back over the Fix tab: it shows which options were right, and why the others fail.
card.ideal: verifies with the exploit before calling it fixed.
